narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, and both pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile after your first year and the bottom decile after your third year, well below the average performance of students who were accepted. These low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that outweighed other information.

Your LSAT score of 38 was the second most important factor. It worked in your favor, pulling the prediction slightly toward passing because it sits just above the average score of accepted students. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your class rankings.

Your upper-middle family income was the third most influential detail. It also nudged the outcome slightly toward success, which is typical for students from that background, but again the benefit was modest.

In short, the model concluded that your relatively weak performance throughout law school made success on the bar exam uncertain enough to deny admission. To improve your chances next time, focus on raising your class standing in future coursework or consider retaking the LSAT to achieve a substantially higher score. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction.
